opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most of the new capabilities will come from the same place they've come from over the past five or six years, which is scale. People sometimes want a more exciting story, some clever architectural breakthrough, but if you look at the historical record, the bulk of the gains have come from throwing more compute at training, along with steady algorithmic efficiency improvements that compound over time. Training compute for frontier models has been growing by roughly four to five times per year, and I don't see an obvious reason for that to stop before the end of the decade. There are constraints on power, chip production, and capital, but none of them seem binding on a five-year horizon.

What I think will change is *what* the compute gets spent on. Pre-training on internet text was the dominant paradigm for a while, and we're running into the limits of high-quality human-written data. So more of the capability gains will come from reinforcement learning, from training models in environments where they actually have to do things: write and debug code, operate a computer, carry out multi-step tasks over hours or days rather than seconds. Building those environments is expensive and labor-intensive, and I suspect that will be one of the real bottlenecks.

On specific capabilities, I'd expect large improvements in long-horizon agency, in coherence over extended tasks, and in the ability to use tools and software reliably. These are things current models are noticeably bad at compared to their raw knowledge or their performance on short benchmark questions. There's a kind of Moravec's paradox here: models can solve hard competition math problems but still struggle to reliably book a flight or manage a messy real-world project. I think closing that gap is where much of the action will be.

That said, I'm somewhat more skeptical than many people in the field about how fast this translates into broad automation. Benchmarks saturate quickly, but economic impact has lagged well behind benchmark performance. My guess is that in five years we'll have systems that are extremely impressive and automate a meaningful share of remote cognitive work, but not systems that can do essentially everything a human worker does. The tasks requiring robust agency, good judgment in unfamiliar situations, and coordination over long time periods are hard, and I expect them to fall more gradually than the most aggressive forecasts suggest.

r001.rationale: The response says scale has driven most gains and downplays the need for a clever architectural breakthrough, but it does not clearly predict that transformer architecture will remain broadly stable.

r002.rationale: It predicts capability gains will increasingly come from reinforcement learning and training models in environments that require tool use and multi-step tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most of the new capabilities over the next five years will come from the same basic recipe that got us here, just pushed further along several axes at once, and I'd separate those axes because they have different dynamics.

The first is just scale, in the old-fashioned sense: more compute, more data, bigger models. I don't think that's finished. Training compute for frontier runs has been growing something like four or five times per year, and the constraints people point to, power, chips, capital, are real but they look like things that slow the growth rate rather than stop it. So you should still expect the pretraining scaling curve to deliver steady improvements in the kinds of things it has always delivered: broader knowledge, better world modeling, fewer silly mistakes. What it probably won't deliver on its own is a discontinuity.

The second axis, and the one I think is doing most of the interesting work right now, is reinforcement learning on top of pretrained models. Once you have a model that's good enough to make non-trivial progress on tasks with verifiable outcomes, math, code, anything where you can check the answer, you can train it directly on whether it succeeded, and you get these very steep improvements in a fairly narrow set of domains. That's what the reasoning models have been. My expectation is that this expands outward from the domains where verification is cheap into domains where it's harder, as people get better at building environments and reward signals for messier tasks. That expansion is the thing to watch, because the pace of progress is going to be very uneven across tasks depending on how easy it is to construct a good training signal.

The third axis is what I'd loosely call agency or long-horizon competence. If you look at the task horizons models can handle autonomously, they've been roughly doubling every several months. If that trend holds, within five years you're talking about systems that can do work that would take a human days or weeks, not minutes or hours. That's a qualitatively different kind of capability, not because the model knows more facts but because it can recover from mistakes, keep track of a goal, and operate in an environment over time. A lot of the economic value is gated on this rather than on raw intelligence, so I think it's the most consequential axis even if it's less glamorous than benchmark scores.

And then there's a set of things I'd call the unglamorous enablers: inference getting much cheaper, context windows getting longer and actually usable, better tool use, multimodality that works reliably. None of these are breakthroughs, but they compound. A model that is only modestly smarter but ten times cheaper and able to run for hours unsupervised looks like a very different product.

Where I'd push back on some of the more dramatic framings is on the idea that we're going to get sudden, unexpected capabilities emerging out of nowhere. Historically, when people have gone back and measured carefully, most of the so-called emergent abilities turned out to be smooth improvements that looked discontinuous because of how they were being evaluated. So my default picture is continuous but fast: steady progress on the pretraining side, uneven and sometimes very rapid progress wherever RL can get a foothold, and task horizons extending in a way that eventually lets these systems substitute for a meaningful fraction of knowledge work. The uncertainty I'd flag is mostly about the RL piece, how far it generalizes beyond the domains where we can verify answers cheaply. If it generalizes well, five years is a long time. If it doesn't, you still get very capable systems, but the gap between what they can do in code and math versus the rest of the economy stays wide for longer than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response describes continuing the current scaling and training recipe, but it does not clearly predict that the transformer architecture itself will remain broadly stable.

r002.rationale: The response identifies continued pretraining scale and reinforcement learning on pretrained models as major sources of new capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the most likely answer is through a combination of scaling and finding better ways to train and use these models. I wouldn’t expect us to need to replace transformers altogether to get substantial improvements over the next five years. But I’m much less confident about exactly which capabilities will emerge, or when.

It helps to distinguish between a model getting better at predicting text and a system getting better at accomplishing a task. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing. You can improve the underlying model with more compute and better data. You can also give it tools, let it spend more time working through a problem, and train it on whether its attempts actually succeed. That creates routes to new capabilities beyond simply making pretraining runs larger.

One particularly interesting possibility is that models become better at producing useful training data for themselves. The constraint there is evaluation: can you tell whether what they’ve produced is correct? If you can check an answer or test a piece of code, there’s a clearer path to improvement than in domains where judging quality is itself difficult.

So I’d expect substantial progress, but uneven progress. A system might become very good at solving fairly difficult, well-defined problems while still struggling with a long project that requires it to make hundreds of decisions reliably. Over five years, I think improving that reliability could matter as much as improving the best answer a model can produce.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it does not expect transformers to be replaced over the next five years, indicating the architecture will remain broadly stable.

r002.rationale: The candidate identifies better training methods, including training on task success and models producing useful training data, as routes to new capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it will come from scaling up the things that already work. You train larger models, you use more compute, you improve the data, and you get systems that can do a wider range of tasks. I don’t think we need to assume some fundamentally new architecture for substantial progress over the next five years.

But I would distinguish between a model acquiring a capability during training and a system becoming capable because we give it more time and better tools. A model might struggle to answer a question immediately, but succeed if it can write code, check its work, and try several approaches. That’s a potentially important source of progress, especially on tasks where you can verify whether an answer is correct.

The harder question is how far those improvements generalize. Getting very good at a benchmark isn’t necessarily the same as being able to carry out a messy project over a week without supervision. Reliability, learning from feedback, and keeping track of what you’re trying to accomplish all matter there.

So I would expect substantial gains, but I’m less confident about exactly when particular capabilities will appear. We have fairly good reasons to expect that spending more resources will improve these systems. Translating that into a precise forecast about what they’ll be able to do in five years is much more uncertain.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects substantial progress without a fundamentally new architecture, implying the transformer architecture will remain broadly stable over the next five years.

r002.rationale: The candidate points to training larger models, using more compute, and improving data as likely sources of new capabilities.
